paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism (AR-JP) is a hereditary neurodegenerative disorder in which parkinsonism responds to levodopa (Matsumine et al., 1997; Saito et al., 1998). Its pathology is a highly selective degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the zona compacta of the substantia nigra (Matsumine et al., 1997). A related presentation, early-onset parkinsonism with diurnal fluctuation (EPDF), is characterized by early onset and improvement of parkinsonian symptoms after sleep, and may follow a benign clinical course (Matsumine et al., 1998).

paragraphs.text: Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996) presented 17 patients from 12 Japanese families with familial juvenile parkinsonism suggesting autosomal recessive inheritance. There was a female predominance, and the mean age at onset was 27.8 years. The symptoms of the parkinsonian triad (tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia) were mild, but gait freezing, hyperreflexia, foot dystonia, and retropulsion were relatively prominent. A characteristic finding was amelioration of parkinsonian symptoms after sleep in all patients. Progression was slow. Response to levodopa was satisfactory, but dopa-induced choreic limb dyskinesia and wearing-off phenomenon occurred frequently. The authors concluded that the similarity of clinical findings among these patients, and their differences from other types of parkinsonism, indicated that AR-JP is a distinct clinical entity.
